# B5. The UK {#oecd-uk}

The UK is calibrated as the U.S. and France are in appendix {{< var p.app_US >}} of the paper, under log preferences,
to its own pension spending, demography, design and average workweek, with the U.S. discount factor imposed. Its
household data are the Harmonised British Household Panel Survey, wave 17, which refers to 2006–07 and is distributed
by the UK Data Service; later waves were collected at least in part during the Great Recession. The income groups are
cut as for the U.S., so that the mean incomes of the low and medium groups are half the mean and the mean. The cuts
set the population shares and the productivities, not the design: θ is the slope of the public pension on earnings,
measured as for every country of the paper's cross-country test (appendix {{< var p.app_oecd26_data >}} of the
paper). The propensities to vote are from the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES). [B1](oecd-ies.qmd) gives
the calibration at every IES of the grid, and [C6](esc-countries.qmd) lets the UK's electorate choose its design.

Table {{< var x.OECD_Calibration >}} sets the UK beside the U.S. and France. Its design is the least Bismarckian of
the three, and its population is older than the U.S. one and younger than France's. Its tax rate is a little above the
U.S. one, while its calibrated political weight of the old is the lowest of the three: in the model an older population
and flatter benefits both raise the tax rate the electorate chooses at a given weight (section {{< var p.sec_LOG >}}
of the paper). The ratio of high to low productivity is close to the U.S. one and well above France's. The common
taste for leisure, pinned by the UK's average workweek relative to the U.S. one, is the highest of the three, almost
twice the U.S. level.

{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD_Calibration.qmd >}}

In table {{< var x.UK_householdheterogeneity >}}, the UK's cuts put fewer households in the low group than the U.S.
cuts do, and most of them in the medium group. The propensity to vote rises with income by less than in the U.S. and by
more than in France, where it is nearly flat (tables {{< var p.table_a_US_CalibUS >}} and
{{< var p.table_a_US_CalibFR >}} of the paper).
